title: What Is Abnormal?
description: Defining mental disorder, the deviance debate, and cultural context

concepts.title: Defining Mental Disorder
concepts.contentHtml:
What separates a mental disorder from ordinary suffering, eccentricity, or deviance? Clinical psychology has used several overlapping criteria.

Statistical infrequency: behaviour or experience that lies far from the population mean. But rarity alone is not pathology — exceptional altruism is also rare.
Deviation from social norms: violation of cultural expectations. But norms vary, and some norms (e.g. about race or sexuality) have themselves been pathologising.
Personal distress: subjective suffering. But some conditions, like mania or anosognosia, may impair the very capacity to feel distressed.
Functional impairment: inability to work, love, or care for oneself. This is the criterion most central to modern diagnosis.

Jerome Wakefield's influential harmful dysfunction account combines a value component (harm) with a factual component (a mental mechanism failing to perform its evolved function).

concepts.title: Models of Pathology
concepts.contentHtml:
How disorder is conceptualised has changed dramatically across history.

The medical model treats mental disorders as diseases analogous to physical ones — disturbances of brain biology to be diagnosed and treated. It dominates modern psychiatry and underwrites pharmacological treatment.

The biopsychosocial model (George Engel, 1977) insists that biology, psychology, and social context interact in any disorder. Depression is not just neurochemistry; it involves cognitions, relationships, and economic conditions.

The diathesis-stress model proposes that disorders emerge when an underlying vulnerability (genetic, temperamental) meets sufficient environmental stress. The same trauma may produce PTSD in one person and not another.

More recently, the network approach (Borsboom) treats disorders not as latent diseases causing symptoms, but as self-reinforcing networks of symptoms causing each other.

concepts.title: Culture and the Construction of Disorder
concepts.contentHtml:
What counts as disorder depends partly on culture. Culture-bound syndromes — koro (genital retraction anxiety in parts of Asia), amok (sudden violent outburst in Southeast Asia), susto (fright sickness in Latin America) — challenge the idea that diagnostic categories are universal.

Even disorders considered universal show striking cultural variation. The presentation of depression differs across cultures: Chinese patients more often report somatic symptoms (fatigue, pain); Western patients more often report psychological ones (sadness, guilt). The Cultural Formulation Interview in DSM-5 acknowledges that diagnosis must consider the patient's framework.

Ethan Watters' Crazy Like Us (2010) argued that the global export of Western diagnostic categories has reshaped how distress is experienced and expressed — a phenomenon sometimes called diagnostic colonialism. The boundary between discovering disorder and constructing it is contested.

title: The DSM and the Project of Diagnosis
description: From DSM-I to DSM-5-TR, the ICD, and the politics of classification

concepts.title: A Brief History of the DSM
concepts.contentHtml:
The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders is published by the American Psychiatric Association. Its evolution mirrors changing assumptions about the mind.

DSM-I (1952) and DSM-II (1968) were thin volumes heavily influenced by psychoanalysis, organising disorders around presumed inner conflicts. Reliability — different clinicians reaching the same diagnosis — was poor.

DSM-III (1980), led by Robert Spitzer, was a paradigm shift. It abandoned aetiological theory in favour of operationalised criteria: explicit checklists of symptoms, durations, and exclusions. This dramatically improved reliability and made psychiatry compatible with research and insurance.

DSM-IV (1994) refined the criteria. DSM-5 (2013) eliminated the multi-axial system and grouped disorders by spectra. DSM-5-TR (2022) updated text and added prolonged grief disorder. The competing system, the WHO's ICD-11 (2022), is used internationally and is broadly compatible.

concepts.title: Categories of Disorder
concepts.contentHtml:
The DSM-5-TR groups hundreds of diagnoses into broad categories. The major ones include:

Mood disorders: major depressive disorder, persistent depressive disorder, bipolar I and II.
Anxiety disorders: generalised anxiety, panic, specific phobias, social anxiety.
Trauma-related: PTSD, acute stress disorder, adjustment disorders.
Obsessive-compulsive: OCD, body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding (separated from anxiety in DSM-5).
Psychotic disorders: schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, brief psychotic disorder.
Personality disorders: borderline, narcissistic, antisocial, avoidant, and others (Cluster A, B, C).
Neurodevelopmental: autism spectrum, ADHD, intellectual disability.
Eating disorders: anorexia, bulimia, binge-eating disorder.

The categorical system has practical advantages but is criticised for treating dimensional phenomena as discrete kinds — most depressive symptoms exist on a continuum with normal sadness.

concepts.title: Reliability, Validity, and the RDoC Alternative
concepts.contentHtml:
A diagnostic system can be reliable (clinicians agree) without being valid (carving nature at its joints). DSM-III achieved reliability; whether the categories are valid biological or psychological kinds is more contested.

Critics note that diagnoses are heavily comorbid (most depressed patients also meet criteria for anxiety), boundaries are fuzzy, and decades of biomarker research have failed to identify reliable biological signatures for most disorders.

In 2013 the US National Institute of Mental Health launched Research Domain Criteria (RDoC): a research framework that abandons DSM categories in favour of transdiagnostic dimensions like negative valence, positive valence, cognitive systems, arousal. The aim is to ground future classification in neurobiology and behaviour rather than committee consensus.

RDoC is a research tool, not a clinical replacement — but its existence signals deep uncertainty about whether DSM categories will survive long-term.

title: Mood, Anxiety, and Psychosis
description: Major disorder families and what is known about them

concepts.title: Depression and Bipolar Disorder
concepts.contentHtml:
Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is diagnosed when five or more symptoms — including depressed mood or anhedonia — persist for at least two weeks and cause functional impairment. Symptoms include sleep disturbance, psychomotor changes, worthlessness, concentration problems, and suicidal ideation. Lifetime prevalence in high-income countries is roughly 15–20%.

The simple monoamine hypothesis — that depression is a serotonin or noradrenaline deficiency — is now considered an oversimplification. Modern accounts emphasise neuroplasticity, HPA-axis dysregulation, inflammation, and learned cognitive patterns.

Bipolar disorder involves alternating episodes of depression and elevated mood. Bipolar I requires at least one manic episode (a week of expansive or irritable mood with grandiosity, decreased sleep, racing thoughts, risky behaviour). Bipolar II involves only hypomania (less severe). Lithium remains the gold-standard mood stabiliser, despite the discovery of its efficacy in 1949 being largely accidental.

concepts.title: Anxiety and Trauma
concepts.contentHtml:
Anxiety disorders are the most prevalent class of mental disorder. Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD) involves persistent, excessive worry about multiple domains. Panic Disorder is defined by recurrent unexpected panic attacks and fear of further attacks. Specific phobias are intense, focal fears (heights, spiders, blood). Social Anxiety Disorder centres on fear of negative evaluation.

Anxiety has clear evolutionary roots — vigilance to threat is adaptive. Disorder arises when the system misfires: detecting danger that is not present, or persisting after threat has passed.

Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), introduced in DSM-III in 1980 partly in response to Vietnam veteran advocacy, requires exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, plus intrusion symptoms (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance, negative cognitions, and hyperarousal lasting more than a month. Complex PTSD (C-PTSD), recognised in ICD-11, captures the additional symptoms following prolonged interpersonal trauma.

concepts.title: Schizophrenia and the Psychotic Spectrum
concepts.contentHtml:
Schizophrenia is defined by the presence of positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech), negative symptoms (flattened affect, avolition, alogia), and significant functional decline lasting at least six months. Lifetime prevalence is roughly 0.5–1%, with onset typically in late adolescence or early adulthood.

It is one of the most heritable psychiatric conditions (twin concordance ~50%), but no single 'schizophrenia gene' exists; hundreds of common variants each contribute small effects, alongside environmental factors like obstetric complications, urban upbringing, and cannabis use in adolescence.

The dopamine hypothesis — that positive symptoms reflect mesolimbic hyperdopaminergia — was inferred from the fact that all effective antipsychotics block D2 receptors and stimulants can induce psychosis. It is partial: it does not explain negative or cognitive symptoms, which respond poorly to current medication.

Outcomes vary widely. Recovery is more common than older textbooks suggested, especially with early intervention.

title: Therapies and Their Evidence
description: CBT, psychodynamic and humanistic therapies, medication, and the empirical record

concepts.title: Cognitive and Behavioural Therapy
concepts.contentHtml:
Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) is the most empirically supported psychotherapy. Its modern form synthesises two traditions.

Behaviour therapy, rooted in learning theory (Wolpe, Skinner), treats disorders by changing reinforcement contingencies and exposure patterns. Exposure therapy for phobias and OCD relies on extinction: prolonged contact with the feared stimulus without the feared outcome reduces conditioned fear.

Cognitive therapy, founded by Aaron Beck in the 1960s, holds that depression and anxiety are maintained by automatic thoughts and cognitive distortions — overgeneralisation, catastrophising, all-or-nothing thinking. Therapy identifies and tests these thoughts against evidence.

Albert Ellis's Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (REBT), developed in 1955, is a parallel ancestor. Its ABC model — Activating event, Beliefs, Consequences — argues that emotional distress flows not from events but from irrational beliefs about events.

Modern third-wave CBTs (ACT, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, DBT) add acceptance and metacognitive elements.

concepts.title: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Approaches
concepts.contentHtml:
Psychodynamic therapy descends from Freud but has evolved considerably. Modern forms emphasise the therapeutic relationship, transference, and unconscious patterns rooted in early relationships. The aim is insight into recurring relational dynamics.

Despite a popular perception that psychodynamic therapy is empirically unsupported, meta-analyses (Shedler 2010; Leichsenring) show robust effects, particularly for personality and complex disorders, with gains persisting after termination. The dominance of CBT in research literature partly reflects ease of manualising — short, structured therapies are easier to study in RCTs than open-ended ones.

Humanistic therapies — Carl Rogers' client-centred therapy, Gestalt, existential therapy — emphasise the inherent capacity for growth. Rogers identified unconditional positive regard, empathy, and congruence as the necessary and sufficient conditions for therapeutic change.

Across approaches, the common factors (alliance, expectation, empathy) often predict outcome better than specific techniques — Bruce Wampold's contextual model.

concepts.title: Medication and the Evidence Base
concepts.contentHtml:
Pharmacotherapy expanded enormously after the 1950s. SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors), introduced with fluoxetine in 1987, became first-line treatment for depression and anxiety. They are safer in overdose than older tricyclics but have modest effect sizes — Cipriani's 2018 network meta-analysis found all 21 antidepressants outperformed placebo, but typically by small margins.

Antipsychotics are divided into first-generation (haloperidol, chlorpromazine — strong D2 blockade, more motor side effects) and second-generation (olanzapine, risperidone, clozapine — broader receptor profile, more metabolic side effects). Clozapine remains uniquely effective for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.

The RCT (randomised controlled trial), pioneered for psychiatric drugs in the 1960s, is the standard for evaluating treatment. Concerns include placebo response inflation, publication bias (Turner 2008 showed unpublished antidepressant trials were largely negative), and the difficulty of blinding when side effects reveal allocation.

For most disorders, combined medication and psychotherapy outperforms either alone.

title: Critiques and Frontiers
description: Antipsychiatry, the limits of pathology, and where clinical psychology is going

concepts.title: Antipsychiatry and Its Heirs
concepts.contentHtml:
Psychiatry has always had radical critics. Thomas Szasz's The Myth of Mental Illness (1961) argued that mental illness is a metaphor: only bodies can be literally sick, and what psychiatry calls illness is really 'problems in living' medicalised to enable social control.

R.D. Laing, in The Divided Self (1960), reframed schizophrenia as an intelligible response to an unliveable family situation. Michel Foucault's History of Madness (1961) traced how the modern category of madness was constructed alongside the asylum, with reason defining itself by excluding what it labelled unreason.

The most cited empirical critique is the Rosenhan experiment (1973): pseudopatients reporting a single auditory hallucination ('thud') were admitted to twelve hospitals and diagnosed with schizophrenia, then took 7–52 days to be discharged despite behaving normally. The study, reported in Science as 'On Being Sane in Insane Places', became a foundational text of antipsychiatry — though Susannah Cahalan's 2019 investigation raised serious doubts about its accuracy.

concepts.title: Diagnostic Controversies
concepts.contentHtml:
Several DSM revisions have been politically and ethically contested.

In 1973, after years of activism led by Frank Kameny and others, the APA voted to remove homosexuality from the DSM. The episode is often cited as evidence that diagnostic categories reflect prevailing values, not just nature. Robert Spitzer, who chaired the change, later said it showed psychiatry could correct itself; critics replied it showed how arbitrary classification can be.

The bereavement exclusion, removed from major depressive disorder in DSM-5 (2013), generated heated debate. Critics including Allen Frances (chair of DSM-IV) argued the change pathologised normal grief; defenders argued severe depressive symptoms after bereavement are still depression and benefit from treatment. DSM-5-TR's prolonged grief disorder reignited the question.

Other recurring controversies: the proliferation of childhood diagnoses (ADHD rates, paediatric bipolar), the categorical/dimensional debate about personality disorders, and pharmaceutical influence on diagnostic boundaries (Healy, Whitaker).

concepts.title: Where Clinical Psychology Is Going
concepts.contentHtml:
Several developments are reshaping the field.

Transdiagnostic approaches: rather than treating each DSM category separately, protocols like Barlow's Unified Protocol target shared mechanisms (emotional avoidance, cognitive rigidity) across anxiety and mood disorders.

Digital and stepped care: internet-delivered CBT (iCBT) has comparable efficacy to face-to-face CBT for many conditions, expanding access dramatically. Stepped-care models match intensity of treatment to severity.

Psychedelic-assisted therapy: trials of psilocybin and MDMA, paired with structured psychotherapy, have shown promise for treatment-resistant depression and PTSD. Methodological challenges around blinding remain serious.

Replication and reform: the replication crisis exposed weaknesses in much clinical research — small samples, flexible analyses, allegiance effects. Pre-registration, larger samples, and routine outcome monitoring (PROMs) are improving rigour.

The discipline still faces foundational questions: are diagnoses natural kinds or pragmatic constructs? Is the goal symptom reduction, functional recovery, or human flourishing? Clinical psychology remains a science continuously negotiating its objects.
